g-prep-11.reason: 'must stay parked' is a durative state continuing to the end of next month, when the work finishes: until. by (deadline for a completed action) does not fit 'stay parked'; since and from need a past/starting point and give no coherent meaning.
g-prep-11.ldbs: L yes (by reads fine in 'lowered by the end of next month'); D yes but marginal (stay is about 7 words before the blank); B no (until/by is a well-drilled pair, stay is a standard cue); S no.
g-prep-11.why: Medium: L and D pass (by survives the window, stay sits just outside it) but B and S fail; good students resolve until/by on stay.
g-prep-11.editorNote: Stem is at the 38-word ceiling; the which-clause about the March inspection adds length but no clue.

g-prep-12.reason: 'within seven days ... of receiving it' is the fixed time-limit frame; the 'of receiving it' that completes it sits after the parenthetical. in seven days ... of is not standard (in marks duration to completion, and 'in ... of' lacks the frame); after contradicts the rejection clause; by seven days of is ungrammatical.
g-prep-12.ldbs: L yes (in and within both fit 'office ___ seven days,'); D yes ('of receiving it' comes after the excluding-public-holidays insertion); B partial (in for a time limit is a real use, but an editor would fix 'in ... of'); S partial (look past the insertion to link within...of). Strict call: medium, not hard, because within is chosen on meaning alone by most good students.
g-prep-12.why: Medium: L and D pass; B and S only borderline since within is the obvious time-limit word.
g-prep-12.editorNote: Not ambiguous: 'in seven days, excluding public holidays, of receiving it' is not formal-standard (colloquial at best). Confidence 4 only because 'in' for a time limit is a real use in other frames.

g-prep-13.reason: 'on the morning of + a specific day' is the standard frame. in the morning is the general frame and is not used with 'of the first day' in formal prose; at the morning is wrong; toward the morning of the first day does not mean 'opens at that time'.
g-prep-13.ldbs: L marginal (in the morning passes in isolation but 'of' is inside the 4-word window and gives the frame away); D no (the cue 'morning of' is adjacent); B partial (in the morning is a habit for some learners); S no. Fails D, and L is borderline, so easy.
g-prep-13.why: Easy: the deciding cue 'morning of the first day' is next to the blank; a learned pattern (on the morning of), no distance.
g-prep-13.fix: Push the cue out and make in/on both plausible, e.g. place a clause between the preposition and 'morning of', or turn it into a different time-preposition pair (at/by/from the start of the first day). toward and at are weak distractors.
g-prep-13.editorNote: In the morning of the first day is attested in literary/other usage; I judge a US or UK editor would change it to on, so not ambiguous. Low risk but note it.

g-prep-14.reason: for eleven consecutive months is the idiomatic duration frame. But 'ran without a single recorded fault during eleven consecutive months before the board agreed ...' is also grammatical and coherent in formal written English: during + NP naming a period (cf. 'fails to pay during two consecutive months' in contracts). An editor may well leave it; since and by are clearly wrong.
g-prep-14.ldbs: L yes (for and during both fit); D no (the numeral phrase 'eleven consecutive months' is in the window and decides it); B no/mixed (during vs for is basic); S no. Fails D, so easy.
g-prep-14.why: Easy: duration word for + length phrase directly after the blank; no distant cue.
g-prep-14.fix: Replace 'during' with a distractor that cannot take a duration, e.g. 'within' (without a single fault within eleven months does not mean the same) or 'at', and if the item needs more weight, push a cue far from the blank. Do not use over/throughout (also pass).
g-prep-14.editorNote: during with a numeral period is grammatical though many editors prefer for; counted as defensible because condition 1 and 2 of 4.1 are both met. Also: since and by are very weak distractors, leaving the item with one real competitor, so fixing it is also a chance to raise difficulty.

g-prep-15.reason: ahead of: sales exceeded the forecast, which 'surprised planners who expected the model to sell slowly' and forced a second shift. in line with is the near-correct distractor (a very natural collocation with forecast), but then sales merely matched the forecast, which would not surprise planners nor trigger a new second shift unless one assumes the forecast was high and the planners disagreed with it. in view of / in spite of do not fit 'run ___ the forecast'.
g-prep-15.ldbs: L yes (run in line with the forecast is a stock phrase and reads perfectly in the window); D yes (the deciding cues, surprised ... expected to sell slowly and second shift, are 10+ words after the blank); B yes (in line with + forecast is a collocation good students trust); S yes (infer direction of the variance from the consequences, no single decisive word). Hard on L/D/B/S, but the exclusion is inferential and depends on an unstated assumption about the forecast's level.
g-prep-15.why: Hard: L, D, B, S all pass; the cues are consequences, not a signal word.
g-prep-15.fix: Make the forecast's level explicit so in line with is clearly excluded: e.g. 'the forecast prepared in January, which assumed the model would sell slowly, and planners must now add a second shift'. Also the relative chain which ... who ... and must ... is clumsy (the subject of 'must now add' is ambiguous); split it.
g-prep-15.editorNote: in line with needs the unstated assumption that the January forecast was optimistic and planners dissented from it; I judge it not defensible, but near enough to merit shouldFix. Stem syntax (which / who / and must) is awkward; style 3.

g-prep-16.reason: throughout the organization = in every part of it, matching 'from the executive floor ... to the smallest depot'. through the organization suggests passage or spread (changes ripple through the organization), not 'applies'; between and toward are wrong in sense.
g-prep-16.ldbs: L doubtful (applies through the organization does not read naturally in the window); D no (the cue from ... to ... is 3 words after); B low (few good students believe through is right); S no. Fails L, so easy.
g-prep-16.why: Easy: throughout the organization is a stock collocation and the only distractor with a trace of plausibility, through, is not convincing with 'applies'.
g-prep-16.fix: Make through a real competitor by using a spread/pass verb context, or change the pair (throughout vs. across / over) with the exclusion in a far clause. toward and between are weak.
g-prep-16.editorNote: I judged 'applies through the organization' not editor-acceptable; low risk of second answer.

g-prep-17.reason: in response to: the output cut follows the reported outage, voluntarily ('rather than waiting for the regulator'). in anticipation of would need the outage to be in the future, but 'was reported last week' presents it as an event that has occurred; in contrast to and in return for are nonsense.
g-prep-17.ldbs: L yes (in anticipation of fits 'trimmed its weekly output ___ the outage'); D yes (the exclusion 'was reported last week' is beyond the 4-word window); B partial (response/anticipation is a classic pair but the past tense of 'reported' is obvious); S no.
g-prep-17.why: Medium: L and D pass; B is weak and S fails.
g-prep-17.fix: Make the outage unambiguously past or ongoing so in anticipation of is firmly out, e.g. 'the outage at Harbor Point that began last week' (not 'was reported', which a reader could take as an announced future outage).
g-prep-17.editorNote: 'an outage that was reported' could be read as a scheduled outage that was announced; this gives in anticipation of a weak reading that needs a mild extra assumption (planned outage), hence shouldFix, not ambiguous.

g-prep-18.reason: out of stock: 'ever since a strike halted production' and the supervisor asking Bexley to fill the order. in stock contradicts both; at stock and by stock are not phrases.
g-prep-18.ldbs: L yes (in stock reads fine in 'have been in stock at the Harlow'); D yes (ever since a strike ... and the Bexley clause are 6+ words after); B no (nobody insists in stock is right once they read on); S no.
g-prep-18.why: Medium (low): L and D pass but B and S fail; the exclusion is plain logic.
g-prep-18.editorNote: Weak distractors: at and by are not live; only in competes. The answer out of is also the only multi-word option, a mild formal giveaway.

g-prep-19.reason: under review is the set phrase (being checked while the legal team checks documents). over review is not English; beyond review would mean impossible to review, contradicting 'the legal team checks'; beside review is nonsense.
g-prep-19.ldbs: L no (over, beside are not plausible; beyond review fits only locally in a grammatical sense and clashes immediately); D no (the cue is the adjacent word 'review' plus a stock phrase); B no; S no.
g-prep-19.why: Easy: a stock collocation with no live distractor.
g-prep-19.fix: Use a set phrase with a live near-competitor and a far cue, e.g. under/in review vs. under/in consideration where the second clause decides, or swap to a more demanding pair.

g-prep-20.reason: in advance of: invoices must be filed before the visit; 'gave the accounts team less than a week to trace the missing receipts' shows the deadline precedes the visit. in the course of (during) is grammatical and meaningful in isolation; in lieu of (instead of) and in the absence of are nonsense.
g-prep-20.ldbs: L yes (in the course of their visit reads fine); D yes (the deciding 'less than a week to trace' follows the comma); B partial (in advance of vs in the course of is a real pair but not one good students strongly believe); S no.
g-prep-20.why: Medium: L and D pass; B weak, S fails.
g-prep-20.fix: Make 'before the visit' unavoidable, e.g. end with 'to trace the missing receipts before anyone from the firm arrived', or replace in the course of with a distractor that cannot be defended (in the wake of would also need checking).
g-prep-20.editorNote: 'asked that invoices be filed in the course of their visit' is odd but not contradicted by 'less than a week to trace' unless one assumes the deadline precedes the visit; this needs an extra assumption, so shouldFix, not ambiguous.

g-prep-21.reason: with regard to: queries about the claim vs. questions 'about the booking itself'. in addition to could parse ('queries in addition to your claim') but makes no sense of the contrast; in accordance with and in the event of are not 'about'.
g-prep-21.ldbs: L no (no distractor reads naturally: 'send any queries in accordance with / in the event of your claim' is wrong at once; in addition to is strained); D partial (contrast comes later but the answer needs no later clue); B no; S no.
g-prep-21.why: Easy: with regard to = about, an obvious fit and no live competitor.
g-prep-21.fix: Use a stem where two multi-word prepositions fit locally and a far cue decides, e.g. in addition to vs. in place of.
g-prep-21.editorNote: The five multi-word sets (g-prep-15, 17, 20, 21, 22) all share the 'in ___ of' format; see overall.

g-prep-22.reason: in charge of: 'once it launches' and 'asked to hand it over to a successor' show he will be running the scheme. in favor of is planted by 'spoken warmly about the plan' and is grammatical, but cannot be handed over; in need of and in case of are nonsense.
g-prep-22.ldbs: L yes (in favor of fits 'will be ___ the pilot scheme'); D yes (the exclusion 'hand it over' is far; 'once it launches' is the near cue); B moderate (the stem plants in favor of, but good students read to the end); S no. Strict: medium, not hard, because 'once it launches' already points to a role.
g-prep-22.why: Medium: L, D pass and B moderate; the misdirection is good but resolves on a close cue.
g-prep-22.editorNote: Best planted distractor in the set; stem is 39 words, one over the 38-word guideline.
